lectures.title: Disk Partitioning with `parted`: CLI Management and Best Practices

cues.en: Now that we have used the user interface for our partitions, let's now have a look at part because
that allows us to manage them through the command line.
So instead of using a user interface, we can also use it on the command line.
We need to start it with a pseudo before because we need additional privileges, of course.
I mean if we are, we are the root user, then of course we don't need the pseudo.
But as a normal user we need a pseudo before we need to be careful with that program.
Though we can easily cause data loss here.
I personally have not used part that often.
Remote servers usually come fully partitioned already and for external drive.
Or if I need to do something on my machine here, I prefer using gparted.
Just because having a nice guy here makes me feel more comfortable and makes me feel more reassured
that I'm not accidentally just deleting my whole system.
Still, this lecture here is really important because, for example, if a server crashes due to some
file system problems, you might need to debug its file systems and you might only have a CLI available.
So this lecture prepares you for the worst case when for example a physical hard drive fails malfunctions
or doesn't work properly, how you can deal with that one.
So let's now have a look at how we can use parted on the command line in our terminal.
So here we are on the command line and I'm now just starting the program parted.
I can just say sudo parted and now we can see here we are now using parted here and right now we are
using dev SDA.
This was my first hard drive in my computer.
We can now use the help command to list the available commands.
We can imagine this as a shell, but not as a bash shell.
It's a different shell.
This is now the parted shell, and we can use this to write commands and then parted will execute them
for us.
So for example, here with help, we get a list here and we can see, for example, we can say print
partitions to display the partition table and to see and to see what's going on.
Or we could use, for example, quit to just exit here our parted program.
So let's now just use the print command.
So for example, here, print partitions and then we can see here it's printing our partitions here,
here, this was print partitions.
Then we can see here dev SDA, this is the device that we are currently working with.
We can see the partition table is GPT and we can see it has two partitions, one here with Fat32 and
the other one with Ext4.
We can also print all of our devices.
So I could say here print devices for example.
And then we would get a list here we got the SDA and the dev SDB device here on our computer because
we have two hard drives here.
If we want to quit parted, we could just use the quit command.
And now you can see we are back in our bash.
I now use the arrow up key to just start parted again.
And let's now have a look at how we could, for example, reset the drive dev SDB, how we could just
wipe it clean and just create a new partition there.
So I use the help command.
We can see here we can select another device here.
So right now we are using dev SDA.
We don't want to delete that one because on that device our system is installed, so we want to just
delete dev SDB.
So I can say I want to select dev SDB.
So from now on I want to work with dev SDB and now I can, for example, print my partitions there again
and we can see here it only has one partition of 50, um, of 52GB.
Why it's not 50GB.
This is because this one here is calculating.
I think it is calculating based on a factor 1000 and not the factor 1024.
So I think this is why it ends up here, but it doesn't really matter.
It gives us a rough idea about the size here.
We can see here, uh, uh, 68.7GB.
And this is the amount of storage associated to this partition here.
We could just delete this partition by using space one to delete this partition.
Or we could also just delete the whole disk.
We can do this with the MK label command, so I can just say MK Label.
I want to create a new partition table.
This will mean that our old partitions are all the data on that disk will be lost.
So I can just say MK label and then it asks us for the new disk label type.
So what kind of partition table we want to use and I want to use the Guid partition table and that's
abbreviated here with GPT.
So we can see here, we need to confirm that everything will be lost on that drive.
So I just confirm that with Yes.
And we can see here now, yeah, everything has been overwritten and I can now, for example, list
my partitions again, I can now say print partitions and we can see here there are no partitions on
my drive.
Now I want to create a new partition, so I use MK part for that so I can say MK part the part type.
The part type is primary because on a GPT partition table we only have primary types anyway.
Uh, so I need to just use primary here then.
The file system type is the file system we want to use that would be ext4.
And then we need to say where our partitions should start and where it should end.
Those numbers are written in megabytes.
So I can say it should start at the beginning and stop at 50,000MB.
Now I can just hit enter and we can see here it's not properly aligned for best performance.
This is because it should match the start should match the physical sectors.
So I will now just cancel that one and we now need to align that properly.
This is just because those those bits might be combined into sectors and it's best if our partition
starts at a logical sector and ends at a logical sector.
So we should not start this at position zero, but we could start this for example at position 2048S
because this tells us that we want to start at at a specific sector and then we can see here everything
is now aligned.
We have lost a little bit of storage capacity, but it's only minimal.
And now we can see the partition is aligned and this will help our drive to be a little bit faster because
otherwise if our program would be like, Hey, we want to just write to this one sector and it would
not match the actual sectors on our drive, then our drive would have to modify two sectors.
But if those sector borders completely align with our file system, it can be a little bit faster.
So this is why I had to align that one.
Another thing that I would like to mention here, instead of the 2048 s or 50,000 here where we define
the start and the end of our partition, we could also just use percentage values here.
For example, we could say this partition should start at 0% to, for example, 70% of our drive and
that would work as well.
If I now print out my partitions again, we can see here it's starting at one at about 2048 sectors.
So we have lost maybe like a megabyte or so, but we can see here this this tradeoff would be worth
it.
And now our petition has been created.
The next thing that we might want to do is that we also give our partition a name.
So for example, here I could name my partition one, for example, I could name it backups and now
I press, I just press enter.
And now I could, for example, print my partitions again.
And we can see here this partition now has a name.
So you can see how we can use this parted program to do all of that for us.
Another way to use the parted program is instead of entering the command line from into the this parted
command line, we can also do everything from the bash.
So we could also say, for example, sudo parted and then we could use parameters here to control it.
So this would, for example, allow us to immediately execute a command.
We have to be even more careful here.
The way to go is that we could, for example, say dash, dash, help to print out how we can use it.
And the syntax here is that we can say sudo parted.
Then we use the device that we want to work with and then just our parted command from our parted shell
that you've seen earlier.
So one way, for example, would be sudo parted.
We wanted to work with Dev SDB on this device and we want to print all partitions.
Then I could use this command here.
Just press enter and then you can see here how it's now here printing our partitions.
So I did not have to enter this parted shell, but I could do everything from my bash.
And yeah, you can imagine this might be convenient sometimes, but sometimes also also the parted shell
might be more convenient.
So this is how we could use the command line to create this partition.
The problem so far is only that we have told the partition table hey the file system there is ext4 but
we haven't actually created that file system.
This is why if we have a look at this partition in gparted, we see here this exclamation sign and it
doesn't really work properly.
Also, if we would now try to access this partition, it would fail.
So we still need to create the actual file system.
So far we have only created the hint which file system we want to use, and for that we need to create
the file system with the following command mkfs dot ext4 because we want to create an ext4 file system
on the following device here.
In that case that would be dev sdb probably sdb1 because that's the first partition of a device usually.
So let's have a look at how we can do this.
So I can say here sudo mkfs dot ext4 slash dev sdb1.
Now everything will be overwritten here, so we do need to confirm that one with a y.
So it's now overwriting that one.
And we can see here a new file system has been created.
We can imagine this a little bit like, okay, before we had created the partition and now we have given
this file system an initial structure so it can now start writing all those folders and all the files
into it.
Now if we would see that in the GUI and I would just refresh my devices here, you can see here we need
about 450MB for that structure, probably also a little bit for the Journal which might be included
here.
The journal means that if we write something to our file system, it will be first written to that journal
in case of power loss.
So the file system has remembered what actions it wants to do next.
And then after it has been written to the journal, it will be applied to the actual data.
And this is great for power loss because if the Journal isn't written completely, we can just forget
about the changes and if it is written completely, then we just apply them later.
So long story short, this is to be expected and everything is working properly here.
So now that we got this volume here, how are we now able to access this volume and for example, write
data to it?
And this will be the topic in the next lecture.
